title: The antibiotic resistance crisis

confidence.note: The warnings, resistance reports and policy milestones are well documented. The death tolls are statistical estimates with wide error bars: the 1.27 million attributable deaths for 2019 carry an uncertainty range of about 0.91 to 1.71 million.

place: Worldwide; action plan adopted at the World Health Assembly, Geneva
people: Alexander Fleming (1881–1955), discoverer of penicillin, who warned of resistance in 1945
summary: Fleming warned in 1945 that misused penicillin would breed resistant germs. By 2019 resistant bacteria were directly killing more than a million people a year.
body: The danger was foreseen at the start. In his Nobel lecture of 11 December 1945, Alexander Fleming warned that once penicillin could be bought in shops, people would underdose themselves and, by exposing their microbes to non-lethal amounts, "make them resistant." The pattern became routine. Penicillin-resistant bacteria had been detected in 1942; methicillin, brought in in 1960 to get around them, met resistance in 1961.

In May 2015 the World Health Assembly adopted a global action plan on antimicrobial resistance, warning of a "post-antibiotic era" in which common infections could kill again, with few replacement drugs in the pipeline. The most comprehensive count to that date followed in 2022: in 2019, resistant bacteria directly caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths and were associated with 4.95 million. A 2024 update put attributable deaths at 1.14 million in 2021 and forecast 39 million deaths attributable to resistance between 2025 and 2050.

In September 2024 the UN General Assembly committed to cutting the 4.95 million deaths a year associated with resistant bacteria by 10% by 2030. In October 2025 WHO reported that one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide in 2023 resisted antibiotic treatment.

links.note: Resistance to penicillin appeared within a few years of its first use.
WHO coordinates the global action plan and resistance surveillance.

title: GLP-1 drugs

confidence.note: Approval dates are on the regulators' record, and the weight and heart benefits come from large randomized trials. What remains uncertain, as WHO noted in 2025, is long-term safety and what happens when people stop.

place: Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston; Novo Nordisk, Denmark
people: Joel Habener, endocrinologist at Massachusetts General Hospital
Svetlana Mojsov, peptide chemist who identified the active form of GLP-1
Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, Novo Nordisk scientist who turned GLP-1 into medicines
summary: A gut hormone found by way of an anglerfish, and a mimic borrowed from a lizard, led to drugs that produce large weight loss, and to a wave of new questions.
body: GLP-1 is a gut hormone that prompts the pancreas to release insulin after a meal. It was found via a fish: in 1982 Joel Habener's laboratory reported that the anglerfish glucagon gene also encodes a second, glucagon-like peptide. In 1987 the chemist Svetlana Mojsov, Habener and Gordon Weir showed that a shortened form, GLP-1 (7-37), is a potent stimulator of insulin release.

The body breaks the hormone down quickly, so the first drug borrowed a sturdier mimic, exendin-4, from the saliva of the Gila monster. Its synthetic copy, exenatide, was approved in 2005. At Novo Nordisk, Lotte Bjerre Knudsen led the work to turn GLP-1 itself into long-acting medicines. Semaglutide, a weekly injection, was approved for diabetes in 2017 and, at a higher dose, for obesity in 2021, after people without diabetes lost on average 15% of their weight.

In March 2024 the FDA approved semaglutide to cut heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths in people with obesity and heart disease, after a trial of more than 17,600 people. In December 2025 WHO issued its first guideline on the drugs for obesity, conditional because long-term data are limited and costs high, and projected that they would reach fewer than 10% of those who could benefit by 2030.

myth.tradition: Ozempic and similar drugs are made from Gila monster venom.
myth.record: Exendin-4 was isolated from the lizard's saliva, not its venom, and a synthetic copy of it became the first GLP-1 drug, exenatide. Semaglutide is a heavily modified form of the human hormone.

links.note: GLP-1 drugs work by boosting the body's own insulin release.

title: COVID-19

confidence.note: The timeline comes from WHO's own records. Death tolls are model estimates that differ by millions between groups, and the virus's origin is unresolved: WHO's advisers judge natural spillover from animals best supported, but say a laboratory leak cannot be ruled out without data China has not shared.

place: First identified in Wuhan, China; worldwide
people: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO
summary: A cluster of 'viral pneumonia' in Wuhan became a pandemic linked to an estimated 15 million excess deaths in two years. Where it came from is still disputed.
body: On 31 December 2019, WHO's office in China picked up a statement from the Wuhan Municipal Health Commission about cases of "viral pneumonia" in the city. On 11 January 2020 WHO said it had received the genetic sequence of the new coronavirus from China. The disease was named COVID-19 in February, and on 11 March 2020, citing "alarming levels of spread and severity" and "alarming levels of inaction", WHO declared that it could be characterized as a pandemic.

Official counts badly understated the toll. WHO later estimated that about 14.9 million more people died in 2020 and 2021 than would otherwise have been expected, directly or indirectly because of the pandemic, with a plausible range of 13.3 to 16.6 million. The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation put the excess at 18.2 million, against 5.94 million reported COVID-19 deaths.

Medicine learned fast by testing. The British RECOVERY trial, run in 176 National Health Service hospital organizations, randomized thousands of patients and showed that dexamethasone, a long-established steroid, cut deaths by about a third among patients on ventilators and by about a fifth among those on oxygen, while offering no benefit to those needing no help breathing. Vaccines followed within the year.

On 5 May 2023 WHO declared that COVID-19 was "an established and ongoing health issue" and no longer a global health emergency. Two years later, on 20 May 2025, the World Health Assembly adopted what WHO called the world's first Pandemic Agreement, after more than three years of negotiation. It cannot be signed until a pathogen-sharing annex is finalized, and by May 2026 member states had agreed to extend those talks.

Where the virus came from remains open. In June 2025 WHO's scientific advisory group concluded that the weight of available evidence suggests spillover from animals, either directly from bats or through an intermediate host. WHO's director-general nonetheless said that all hypotheses, including a laboratory leak, must stay on the table, and asked China again for early genetic sequences and details of animals sold in Wuhan's markets.

myth.tradition: The origin of the virus has been settled, either as a proven laboratory leak or as a proven market spillover.
myth.record: Neither is proven. WHO's advisory group in 2025 judged animal spillover best supported by the available evidence, while WHO said a lab leak could not be excluded without more data from China.

links.note: The last pandemic on a comparable scale.
An earlier coronavirus outbreak that shaped how SARS-CoV-2 was recognized and named.
The pandemic was the first large-scale test of mRNA vaccines.
RECOVERY showed how fast large randomized trials can settle treatment questions.

title: mRNA vaccines

confidence.note: The science and approval dates are well documented, and the Nobel committee's account is authoritative. Lives-saved figures are model-based counterfactuals, cover all COVID-19 vaccines rather than mRNA alone, and depend on which death counts are used.

place: University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia; vaccines authorized worldwide
people: Drew Weissman (b. 1959), immunologist at the University of Pennsylvania
summary: A biochemist who struggled for funding and an immunologist found how to slip synthetic mRNA past the immune system. Fifteen years later it became a pandemic vaccine.
body: Messenger RNA carries a gene's instructions to the protein-making machinery of the cell, and by the 1990s a few researchers hoped to inject it as a medicine. The obstacles were serious. Synthetic mRNA was considered unstable and hard to deliver, needing sophisticated lipid carrier systems developed by others, and it set off inflammation. One of the few who persisted was the Hungarian biochemist Katalin Karikó, an assistant professor at the University of Pennsylvania who had trouble persuading funders that the project mattered.

With a new colleague, the immunologist Drew Weissman, she noticed that the RNA in mammalian cells carries chemically modified bases, while mRNA made in the test tube does not. When they built mRNA with modified bases, the inflammatory response almost disappeared. They published in 2005, and in 2008 and 2010 showed that the modifications also raised protein production.

When the genetic sequence of the new coronavirus reached WHO on 11 January 2020, the platform was ready. Two base-modified mRNA vaccines encoding the virus's surface protein were developed at what the Nobel committee called record speed, reported protection of around 95%, and were approved in December 2020, less than a year after the sequence was shared. On 31 December 2020 WHO issued its first emergency use validation for a COVID-19 vaccine.

Karikó and Weissman shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. By then more than 13 billion doses of COVID-19 vaccines of all types had been given. One modelling study estimated that vaccination prevented 14.4 million COVID-19 deaths in its first year, or 19.8 million if excess deaths are used as the measure. Such figures rest on assumptions about what would otherwise have happened, and they credit all vaccine types, not mRNA alone.

myth.tradition: The mRNA vaccines were an untested technology invented from scratch in a few months.
myth.record: The speed rested on decades of work on mRNA, including Karikó and Weissman's 2005 discovery, published fifteen years before the pandemic. What was compressed was the timetable for testing and manufacture.

links.note: The pandemic that made mRNA vaccines a mass technology.
An older vaccination triumph, achieved over decades rather than months.
Molecular biology tools that made synthetic mRNA possible.

title: AlphaFold and AI in medicine

confidence.note: Regulatory decisions, publications and the Nobel Prize are on record. How much these tools improve patients' outcomes is far less settled: many have been authorized on accuracy studies, and independent checks have sometimes found them much weaker than advertised.

people: Demis Hassabis (b. 1976), chief executive of Google DeepMind
John Jumper (b. 1985), senior research scientist at DeepMind who shared the Nobel for AlphaFold2
Michael Abràmoff, lead investigator of the IDx-DR pivotal trial
summary: Software that learns from examples began reading eye scans unsupervised in 2018 and predicting the shapes of proteins in 2020. Proving it helps patients is harder.
body: Deep learning, software that learns patterns from large sets of labeled examples, entered the clinic through images. In 2018 the FDA authorized IDx-DR, which checks retinal photographs for diabetic eye disease, after a trial of 900 people at primary care clinics. The trial's authors describe it as the first autonomous AI diagnostic system the FDA had authorized in any field of medicine, meaning no clinician had to read the image. By mid-2026 the FDA's public list of AI-enabled devices ran to more than 1,600 entries, three-quarters of them in radiology.

In 2020 Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of DeepMind presented AlphaFold2, which predicts a protein's three-dimensional shape from its amino acid sequence, a problem researchers had attacked since the 1970s. It has since predicted the structures of virtually all 200 million known proteins, and in 2024 it won them a share of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Evidence of patient benefit has lagged behind the promise. When University of Michigan researchers tested a widely used commercial sepsis-warning model in 2021, it missed 67% of sepsis cases while raising alerts on 18% of all hospitalized patients.

links.note: Sequence databases gave AI the raw material to learn from.

title: The first malaria vaccines

confidence.note: WHO's recommendations and Gavi's rollout figures are documented. The vaccines' protection is real but partial, and requires several doses.

place: Ghana, Kenya and Malawi (pilots); sub-Saharan Africa
summary: After 30 years of development, WHO recommended the first malaria vaccine in 2021. A second followed in 2023, and by 2026 doses had reached 25 African countries.
body: On 6 October 2021 WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 for children in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission. It was the product of 30 years of work by GSK with the nonprofit PATH and African research centers. Pilots in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi had reached more than 900,000 children since 2019 and cut deadly severe malaria by 30%. In October 2023 WHO recommended a second vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, partly because demand for malaria vaccines was unprecedented and the supply of RTS,S was limited. Routine vaccination spread from 2024, when Cameroon and 13 other countries began; by January 2026 Gavi had delivered over 39 million doses to 25 African countries.

links.note: The leading malaria drug, which the vaccines complement.

title: Pig organs in people

confidence.note: Each operation was announced by the hospital and has been described in the medical literature. Only a handful of patients have been treated, so how well pig organs work in the long run is still unknown.

people: David Bennett Sr. (d. 2022), first recipient of a gene-edited pig heart
Richard Slayman (d. 2024), first living recipient of a gene-edited pig kidney
summary: In 2022 a dying man received a gene-edited pig's heart and lived two months. By 2025 a pig kidney had kept a man off dialysis for 271 days, bridging him to a human kidney.
body: On 7 January 2022 surgeons at the University of Maryland gave David Bennett, 57, who was too sick for a human heart, a genetically modified pig heart. It worked without immediate rejection; he died on 8 March. On 16 March 2024 Massachusetts General Hospital gave Richard Slayman, 62, a kidney from a pig with 69 genetic edits, the first in a living person. He died within two months of a cardiac event that autopsy did not trace to a heart attack. In 2025 Tim Andrews's pig kidney kept him off dialysis for 271 days, the longest reported, before a human kidney in January 2026. FDA-approved trials are under way.

title: The first drugs to slow Alzheimer's

confidence.note: The approvals are on the FDA's record. Whether the benefit matters to patients is actively debated: the measured slowing is statistically clear but small, below common estimates of a difference patients and doctors would notice.

summary: Antibodies that clear amyloid from the brain became the first drugs shown to slow Alzheimer's. The slowing is real but small, and the side effects can be serious.
body: In June 2021 the FDA gave accelerated approval to aducanumab, an antibody against amyloid, the protein that forms plaques in Alzheimer's brains, despite conflicting trial results: one phase 3 trial positive, one negative. Firmer evidence came with lecanemab, given traditional approval on 6 July 2023 after an 18-month trial in 1,795 patients showed slower decline, and donanemab, approved on 2 July 2024. The FDA called lecanemab's benefit clinically meaningful, but the effect is modest: a pooled analysis of eight trials put it at about a third of a point on a standard dementia rating scale, below common thresholds for a noticeable difference. Both drugs can cause ARIA, brain swelling and small bleeds seen on scans.

links.note: Alzheimer first described the plaques these drugs target.
The drugs are engineered monoclonal antibodies.
